subject: Engineering Fundamentals
title: Fatigue Failure: Death by a Million Tiny Cracks
description: A quick win: understand Fatigue Failure: Death by a Million Tiny Cracks.

hook.text: Bend a paperclip back and forth and it snaps. The metal didn't weaken — microscopic cracks grew until it broke.

buildup.text: Fatigue failure happens below a material's yield stress. Each load cycle extends tiny cracks a microscopic amount.

discovery.text: An S-N curve maps how many cycles a material survives at each stress level. Lower stress means more cycles.

twist.text: Steel has an endurance limit — below a threshold stress, it can survive infinite cycles. Aluminum does not. It always fails.

climax.text: Aircraft are inspected for fatigue cracks constantly. The Aloha Airlines roof failure in 1988 was missed fatigue damage.

punchline.text: Strong enough for one load. But a million loads? That's different.

quiz.question: Why is fatigue more dangerous in aluminum than in steel structures?
options: Aluminum corrodes faster creating stress concentration points
Aluminum has no endurance limit and will always eventually fail under cyclic loads
Aluminum is more brittle and cracks spread faster once they start
